newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Costly new Rolls undermines Vickers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Costly new Rolls undermines Vickers.

text.p: British auto and defence manufacturer Vickers Plc posted a gain in half-year profits on Thursday but admitted it was still struggling to offset the high investment costs required for a new Rolls-Royce car and to get on top of some of its markets.

The group reported an 18 percent rise in first-half pretax profit to 31.8 million pounds, ($50 million) and said it was confident of being able to make further earnings progress in the second half of the year.

However, it also acknowleged that profit margins in its high-profile automotive businesses, including Rolls-Royce and Bentley cars and its specialist engineering firm Cosworth, were pressured both by high investment costs and mixed markets.

Share analysts found the results less bouyant than they had hoped for, with the increased dividend of 2.7 pence per share falling just under the consensus forecast of a jump to 2.8 pence from 2.4 pence a year ago.

The also expressed concern at the slow prospects for new tank orders for Vickers' defence systems division, which chief executive Sir Colin Chandler said was "out there fighting" for prospective Middle Eastern orders, in particular.
Chandler told Reuters he was quietly confident in the company's overall performance but repeated his often-heard warning that "one shouldn't stoke up too many expectations".

"This performance, usefully ahead of the comparable period for last year, represents a process of consolidation during a period of investment for the future," Vickers chairman Sit Richard Lloyd summarised in his statement.
Within an 11 percent rise in total group sales, to 553.8 million pounds, Rolls Royce Motor Cars posted a 26 percent sales rise in the period.
However, Chandler said the unit was under some pressure as it spends on engineering and tooling for its new product line.
"We are investing a lot at the moment...when doing that we obviously are not getting a very good return on sales," he told Reuters in a telephone interview.
Going forward, he added, Rolls's sales prospects would be dependent on the rate of increase of global GDP, which on current forecasts appears to be on a steady course.

"I think we'll see pretty steady growth," he said, though he added Vickers expected the new four-door Bentley and Rolls-Royce model range would spur along sales and allow them to break out of the expected gentle uptrend.
"What will help is the new model, because we believe there is pent-up demand. We do see some good growth," he said.
The profit margin dilution caused by the automotive division's sustained capital expenditure has also had an impact on cashflow, Chandler acknowleged.
In the six months to the end of June, Vickers slipped to being slightly geared, at 8.0 percent, from having net cash.
The group also announced a series of top board changes, which will mean it has to hire a new chief executive and a new chief financial officer during the coming 18 months.
Chandler will become first the deputy chairman, as of today, and then chairman in April next year, retaining his chief executive's post for about another year thereafter.
"The plan is for me to keep both jobs for about a year. During that time we will start a process to look for a new chief executive," he said.
Meanwhile, finance chief Roger Head is to step down from the board at the end of December, after 10 years at his post.

By 1315 GMT, Vickers shares had fallen 11 pence to 260-1/2 pence in fairly brisk trade. Analysts said they had risen quite strongly in the last week partly anticipating upbeat results. ($1=.6373 Pound)
